claim: An optical-genetic toolkit was developed to 'read' neural population responses using widefield calcium imaging while simultaneously using optogenetics to 'write' neural responses into V1 of behaving macaques.
source: To address this question, we developed an optical-genetic toolkit to 'read' neural population responses using widefield calcium imaging, while simultaneously using optogenetics to 'write' neural responses into V1 of behaving macaques.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the development of the toolkit and describes its dual capabilities for reading and writing neural responses.

claim: Detection of a dim target is significantly reduced by a co-localized medium-brightness mask, a phenomenon known as visual masking.
source: We focused on the phenomenon of visual masking, where detection of a dim target is significantly reduced by a co-localized medium-brightness mask (Cornsweet and Pinsker, 1965; Whittle and Swanston, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work establishing visual masking as a known phenomenon.

claim: Low-power optostimulation can significantly reduce visual detection sensitivity, similar to a visual mask.
source: We find that, similar to a visual mask, low-power optostimulation can significantly reduce visual detection sensitivity
evidence: The abstract presents this as a main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: A sublinear interaction between visual- and optogenetic-evoked V1 responses could account for the perceptual masking effect.
source: that a sublinear interaction between visual- and optogenetic-evoked V1 responses could account for this perceptual effect
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding based on neural measurements during the experiments.

claim: The neural and behavioral masking effects of optostimulation are spatially selective.
source: and that these neural and behavioral effects are spatially selective.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data comparing effects at different spatial locations.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation in early sensory cortex has been demonstrated to cause clear neural effects in NHPs.
source: For example, while optostim in early sensory cortex has been demonstrated to cause clear neural (e.g., Ju et al., 2018; Ruiz et al., 2013; Nassi et al., 2015; Jazayeri et al., 2012; May et al., 2014; Andrei et al., 2019) and behavioral (e.g., Ju et al., 2018; Jazayeri et al., 2012; May et al., 2014; Andrei et al., 2019) effects in NHPs
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous optostimulation experiments in NHPs typically require high-power optostimulation (10s to 100s of mW/mm2).
source: such experiments typically require high-power optostimulation (10s to 100s of mW/mm2)
evidence: The claim is based on a review of previous literature in the field.

claim: Viral-based methods were developed for stable long-term co-expression of GCaMP6f and C1V1 in excitatory V1 neurons.
source: First, we developed viral-based methods for stable long-term co-expression of a calcium indicator (GCaMP6f; Chen et al., 2013) and a red-shifted opsin (C1V1; Packer et al., 2012) in a population of excitatory V1 neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of methods and reference to Figure 2A showing the expression.

claim: A widefield imaging system was developed that allows simultaneous optostimulation and imaging of NHP cortex with negligible cross-talk.
source: Second, we developed a widefield imaging system that allows us to simultaneously optostimulate and image NHP cortex with negligible cross-talk between these optical read/write components (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the imaging system and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The response of neurons in the visual cortex to visual stimuli is highly nonlinear.
source: The response of neurons in the visual cortex to visual stimuli is highly nonlinear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about visual cortex responses.

claim: The response to a stimulus at 100% contrast is typically much lower than twice the response at 50% contrast.
source: For example, the response to a stimulus that is at 100% contrast is typically much lower than twice the response at 50% contrast (Albrecht and Hamilton, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The threshold for detecting a dim visual target is low on a uniform gray background.
source: The threshold for detecting a dim visual target is low on a uniform gray background (Figure 1B, top)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B demonstrating this phenomenon.

claim: Detection threshold is significantly higher when a dim target is added to a co-localized medium-brightness pedestal mask.
source: and significantly higher when it is added to a co-localized medium-brightness pedestal mask (Figure 1B, bottom), consistent with Weber's law (Cornsweet and Pinsker, 1965).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B and citations to previous work.

claim: AAV1-CaMKIIa-NES-GCaMP6f viral vector was used for GCaMP6f expression in Monkey L.
source: For neural reading, each monkey was first injected with ~2 µl of a GCaMP6f (Chen et al., 2013) viral vector per injection site (Monkey L with AAV1-CaMKIIa-NES-GCaMP6f [Deisseroth lab], and Monkey T with AAV1-CaMKIIa-GCaMP6f [Zemelman lab]).
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the viral vectors used.

claim: The GCaMP6f virus leads to expression in ~90% of excitatory neurons in macaque V1.
source: Our previous work revealed that this virus leads to GCaMP expression in ~90% of excitatory neurons in macaque V1 (Seidemann et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Initial expression of GCaMP6f was observed at around 6–10 weeks post injection.
source: Initial expression of GCaMP6f was observed at around 6–10 weeks post injection.
evidence: The methods section reports this observation from the experiments.

claim: Stable functional GCaMP6f response levels were reached 4–8 weeks after initial expression.
source: Stable functional response levels were reached 4–8 weeks after (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: GCaMP6f expression lasted for the lifespan of the imaging chambers (>2 years in both monkeys).
source: and lasted for the lifespan of the chamber (>2 years in both monkeys).
evidence: The methods section reports the duration of stable expression.

claim: AAV5-CaMKIIa-C1V1(t/t)-TS-eYFP viral vector was used for C1V1 expression in both monkeys.
source: This viral vector contained a red-shifted ChR-based opsin C1V1 (Packer et al., 2012) (AAV5-CaMKIIa-C1V1(t/t)-TS-eYFP [Deisseroth lab] for both monkeys).
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the viral vector used.

claim: Initial C1V1 expression was observed 4–6 weeks post injection.
source: Initial C1V1 expression was observed 4–6 weeks post injection
evidence: The methods section reports this observation from the experiments.

claim: Stable functional C1V1 response levels were obtained 4–8 weeks after initial expression.
source: and again took 4–8 weeks for stable functional response levels to be obtained (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The eYFP emission spectrum overlaps with that of GCaMP, leading to elevated baseline fluorescence at the co-expression site.
source: Because the eYFP emission spectrum overlaps with that of GCaMP, the baseline fluorescence (F) at the co-expression site was significantly elevated after the C1V1 expression
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments, based on known spectral properties.

claim: The change in fluorescence (∆F) in response to visual stimulus remained comparable at C1V1 and GCaMP-only sites.
source: However, the change in fluorescence in response to the visual stimulus (∆F) remained comparable at the two sites (Figure 1C, middle), indicating stable expression of both the GCaMP and C1V1
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C (referenced as Figure 2C in the text).

claim: The size of the area activated by optogenetic stimulation was ~2 mm2 at half of the maximal response.
source: The size of the area activated by optogenetic stimulation was ~2 mm2 at half of the maximal response.
evidence: This is reported as a measurement from the experiments.

claim: The optostimulation-activated area contains several hundred thousand neurons.
source: This area contains several hundred thousand neurons (Kelly and Hawken, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to previous work on neuron density.

claim: Optostim-driven responses could only be measured at the C1V1 site, not at the GCaMP-only site.
source: Even though the stimulation light covered both sites, optostim-driven responses could only be measured at the C1V1 site (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The optical stimulation light at 580 nm was efficiently blocked from contaminating GCaMP imaging measurements.
source: This confirms that the optical stimulation light (at 580 nm) was efficiently blocked from contaminating our GCaMP imaging measurements (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the observation that only the C1V1 site showed optostim responses.

claim: Robust GCaMP responses to optostim were observed at peak power densities below 1 mW/mm2.
source: Pilot imaging experiments revealed robust GCaMP responses to optostim at peak power densities below 1 mW/mm2 that were within the ballpark of the visual-evoked responses.
evidence: This is reported as an observation from pilot experiments.

claim: For Monkey L, optostim was tested at peak power levels of 0.6 and 1.2 mW/mm2.
source: Therefore, for Monkey L, we chose to test the behavioral and neural effect of optostim at peak power levels of 0.6 and 1.2 mW/mm2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental parameter choice.

claim: The blue GCaMP excitation light can affect the monkey's detection performance due to the broad excitation spectra of C1V1.
source: Pilot detection experiments revealed that, due to the broad excitation spectra of C1V1 (Packer et al., 2012), the blue GCaMP excitation light can affect the monkey's detection performance (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by pilot experimental data shown in the referenced figure and citation to C1V1 properties.

claim: Blue light level was minimized to 0.05 mW/mm2 in Monkey L and 0.01 mW/mm2 in Monkey T.
source: We therefore minimized the blue light level to 0.05 mW/mm2 in Monkey L and 0.01 mW/mm2 in Monkey T by running the camera at a low frame rate (20 Hz) and at a very low saturation level
evidence: This is stated as an experimental parameter adjustment.

claim: The monkeys' behavioral thresholds with low-level blue light were comparable to their thresholds during training without blue light.
source: The monkeys' behavioral thresholds with the low-level blue light were comparable to their thresholds during training without blue light.
evidence: This is reported as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Under the tested conditions, the cross-talk between optical 'read' and optical 'write' components is negligible.
source: Therefore, under the conditions tested here, the cross-talk between the optical 'read' and optical 'write' components in our system is negligible.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the behavioral threshold comparisons.

claim: Two macaque monkeys were trained to perform a reaction-time visual detection task.
source: To test the hypothesis that low-power optostim can substitute for a visual mask and cause a significant decrease in neural and behavioral detection sensitivities, we trained two macaque monkeys to perform a reaction-time visual detection task (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as part of the experimental design.

claim: A visual target (a small white Gaussian stimulus; 0.33° FWHM) appeared at a known location on half of the trials.
source: A visual target (a small white Gaussian stimulus; 0.33° FWHM) appeared at a known location on half of the trials.
evidence: This is stated as part of the experimental design.

claim: Monkeys indicated target presence by making a saccade to the target location and target absence by maintaining fixation.
source: To receive a reward, the monkey had to indicate the presence of the target by making a saccade to the target location on target-present trials, or to maintain fixation on target-absent trials
evidence: This is stated as part of the behavioral task design.

claim: In optostim blocks, optostim was applied on every trial, acting as a substitute for the visual mask.
source: Note that in the optostim blocks, optostim acted as a visual mask (i.e., a co-localized baseline visual stimulus that appears on all trials; Figure 1B, bottom) and the monkey had to discriminate between trials with optostim only and trials in which the visual stimulus and optostim input coincided.
evidence: This is stated as part of the experimental design.

claim: Optostim was applied in 5 ms pulses at 44 Hz.
source: Optostim was applied in 5 ms pulses at 44 Hz
evidence: This is stated as an experimental parameter.

claim: Optostim onset was delayed 40 ms relative to visual target onset to compensate for the latency of visual responses.
source: optostim onset was delayed 40 ms relative to visual target onset to compensate for the latency of the visual responses so that response onset to the visual target and to optostim coincided
evidence: This is stated as an experimental design choice with rationale.

claim: Optostim caused a large perceptual masking effect that led to a reduction in the monkey's ability to detect the visual target.
source: Consistent with the second hypothesis, we found that optostim caused a large perceptual masking effect that led to a reduction in the monkey's ability to detect the visual target in the presence of optostim (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a main finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Across all experiments in Monkey L, optostim at 0.6 mW/mm2 caused a large drop in bias-adjusted accuracy.
source: Across all experiments in Monkey L, optostim at 0.6 mW/mm2 caused a large drop in the monkey's bias-adjusted accuracy (Figure 3C; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for a non-bias-adjusted version of the figure)
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: In Monkey L, optostim caused primarily a large drop in hit rate and much smaller increase in false alarm rate.
source: In this monkey, optostim caused primarily a large drop in hit rate (Figure 3A) and much smaller increase in false alarm rate (one minus correct rejections rate) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Increasing optostim peak power density to 1.2 mW/mm2 caused a further decrease in accuracy and increase in detection threshold.
source: Increasing the optostim peak power density to 1.2 mW/mm2 caused a further decrease in accuracy and an increase in detection threshold.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Optostim caused a significant reduction in the monkey's detection criterion at the higher power density.
source: In addition to a significant increase in detection threshold, optostim also caused a significant reduction in the monkey's detection criterion at the higher power density (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: The criterion adjustment by the monkey was insufficient to fully compensate for the perceptual consequences of optostim.
source: In other words, the results suggest that the monkey's criterion adjustment was insufficient to fully compensate for the perceptual consequences of the optostim.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the criterion shift results.

claim: A similar large perceptual masking effect of optostim was observed in Monkey T.
source: A similar large perceptual masking effect of optostim was observed in Monkey T (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figure 3F-J.

claim: In Monkey T, even optostim at 0.3 mW/mm2 caused a significant increase in detection threshold.
source: Because the behavioral effects of optostim at 0.6 mW/mm2 were already high, we also tested the effect of optostim at 0.3 mW/mm2. Even at this low-power level, we observed a significant increase in detection threshold in the presence of optostim.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: In Monkey T, optostim caused mainly an increase in false alarm rate and a smaller drop in hit rate.
source: In this monkey, optostim caused mainly an increase in the false alarm rate and a smaller drop in hit rate
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: In Monkey T, optostim caused a significant reduction in the monkey's detection criterion.
source: and a significant reduction in the monkey's detection criterion.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Low-power optostim in macaque V1 can substitute for a visual mask and cause large behavioral masking effects.
source: Thus, our results reveal that low-power optostim in macaque V1 can substitute for a visual mask and cause large behavioral masking effects.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The effect of optostim on the monkeys' reaction times were weak and variable.
source: In contrast to the large and significant effect of optostim on the monkey's detection performance, the effect of optostim on the monkey's reaction times were weak and variable (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: No clear effect of optostim on the end points of the monkeys' saccades toward the target was observed.
source: Similarly, we did not observe a clear effect of optostim on the end points of the monkeys' saccades toward the target (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: Optostim had a much smaller effect when the target was presented at the visual field location corresponding to the GCaMP-only site.
source: Despite the fact that optostim light covered both the C1V1 and the GCaMP-only sites, and that the receptive fields at the two locations partially overlapped (see Materials and methods), optostim had a much smaller effect when the target was presented at the visual field location corresponding to the GCaMP-only site (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The behavioral effect of optostim is spatially selective, consistent with optostim acting as a visual mask rather than as a general distracter.
source: These results show that the behavioral effect of optostim is spatially selective, consistent with the hypothesis that optostim is acting as a visual mask rather than as a general distracter.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the spatial selectivity findings.

claim: Widefield GCaMP signals are approximately linearly related to the locally pooled spiking activity in macaque V1.
source: Our previous work (Seidemann et al., 2016) demonstrates that widefield GCaMP signals, which measure the pooled activity of populations of neurons in a Gaussian shaped region with a space constant of ~0.2 mm (Chen et al., 2012), are approximately linearly related to the locally pooled spiking activity in macaque V1.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: Any sublinear interaction between visual- and optogenetic-evoked GCaMP responses is likely to reflect sublinear interaction at the level of V1 spiking activity.
source: Therefore, any sublinear interaction between visual- and optogenetic-evoked GCaMP responses is likely to reflect sublinear interaction at the level of V1 spiking activity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the known relationship between GCaMP signals and spiking activity.

claim: In one experiment in Monkey L, both the visual target at 50% Weber contrast and direct optogenetic stimulation produced similar amplitude responses (Ropto/Rvis50 = 0.95).
source: In the first experiment, both the visual target (at 50% Weber contrast) and direct optogenetic stimulation produced similar amplitude responses (Figure 5A and B; the ratio of response to optostim and visual stim at 50% contrast was Ropto/Rvis50 = 0.95).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a specific experiment, supported by data in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The visual-evoked response in the presence of optostim mask was significantly reduced, consistent with sublinear interaction.
source: The response was stronger when the visual stimulus and the optostim mask were presented simultaneously (Figure 5C), but the visual-evoked response in the presence of the optostim mask was significantly reduced (Figure 5D), consistent with the hypothesis that these two signals interact sublinearly in V1.
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Optostim caused a large reduction (average 50.4%) in visual-evoked responses at all target amplitudes in one experiment.
source: Finally, to measure the overall reduction in the visual-evoked responses in the presence of the optostim, we computed the average visual-evoked response, with and without optostim, at five target amplitudes (Figure 5F; see Materials and methods). Optostim caused a large reduction in the visual-evoked responses at all target amplitudes (average reduction of 50.4%).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figure 5F.

claim: In a second experiment 6 weeks later, the optostim-evoked response was much larger than the visually evoked response (Ropto/Rvis50 = 3.11).
source: In a second experiment conducted 6 weeks later, the optostim at the same power level produced a response that was much larger than the visual-evoked response (Figure 5G; Ropto/Rvis50 = 3.11)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a specific experiment, supported by data in Figure 5G.

claim: The increase in optostim-evoked response over time suggests a possible increase in C1V1 expression level.
source: suggesting a possible increase in the C1V1 expression level between these two experiments (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for the time course of Ropto/Rvis50).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observed increase in response, supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: The reduction of visual-evoked response in the presence of optostim was larger in the second experiment, leading to almost complete elimination of visual-evoked responses.
source: Consistent with higher level of C1V1, the reduction of the visual-evoked response in the presence of optostim was also larger (Figure 5H), leading to almost complete elimination of the visual-evoked responses in the presence of the optostim mask.
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figure 5H.

claim: The behavioral effect of optostim in the second experiment (64% increase in detection threshold) was larger than in the first experiment (35% increase).
source: Similarly, the behavioral effect of optostim in the second experiment (64% increase in detection threshold) was larger than in the first experiment (35% increase in detection threshold).
evidence: This is stated as a finding comparing behavioral effects across experiments.

claim: A summary of physiological results reveals a strong masking effect of optostim on V1 responses.
source: A summary of the physiological results (Figure 6) reveals a strong masking effect of optostim on V1 responses
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: In Monkey T, even the lowest power level of 0.3 mW/mm2 almost abolished all visual-evoked GCaMP responses.
source: which is even stronger in Monkey T, where even the lowest power level of 0.3 mW/mm2 almost abolished all visual-evoked GCaMP responses (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figures 6C-D.

claim: Optostimulation tends to increase response variability, but this effect is not present in all experiments.
source: Analysis of the effect of optostim on the variability of the GCaMP-evoked responses shows that optostim tends to increase response variability, but this effect is not present in all experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: Little or no effect of optostim on visual-evoked response was found at the GCaMP-only site.
source: We find little or no effect of optostim on the visual-evoked response at the GCaMP-only site even though we could still measure a weak optostim-evoked response (average Ropto/Rvis5o=0.33 at this site).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: The weak optostim response at the GCaMP-only site could reflect direct optogenetic activation of horizontal axons or spread of neural responses through horizontal connections.
source: This weak optostim response could reflect a mixture of direct optogenetic activation of horizontal axons originating from the C1V1 site and reaching the GCaMP-only site and/or spread of neural responses elicited by optogenetic stimulation at the C1V1 site through horizontal connections.
evidence: This is stated as a possible interpretation of the weak response observed.

claim: The observed physiological specificity is consistent with the specificity of the behavioral effect.
source: Overall, the observed physiological specificity is consistent with the specificity of the behavioral effect (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion linking physiological and behavioral findings.

claim: The cranial window approach allows viral injections under visual guidance and real-time monitoring of viral spread.
source: This approach has multiple advantages. For example, it allows us to perform viral injections under visual guidance and to monitor in real-time the viral spread (Seidemann et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the experimental approach, with citation to previous work.

claim: The cranial window approach allows imaging to confirm GCaMP and opsin expression in parallel across multiple injection sites.
source: to use imaging to confirm the GCaMP and opsin expression in parallel and across multiple injections sites
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the experimental approach.

claim: The cranial window approach allows monitoring of long-term stability of expression.
source: to monitor the long-term stability of the expression
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the experimental approach.

claim: The cranial window approach allows calibration of stimulation parameters based on optically measured neural responses.
source: and to calibrate the stimulation parameters based on the optically measured neural responses.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the experimental approach.

claim: The eYFP tag attached to C1V1 creates a fluorescent baseline that reduces the functional GCaMP signal.
source: One weakness of the current opsin construct is that the eYFP tag that is attached to C1V1 creates a fluorescent baseline that reduces the functional GCaMP signal (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current approach, supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: Future use of an opsin with a red static fluorescent tag will address the issue of eYFP interference with GCaMP.
source: Future use of an opsin with a red static fluorescent tag will address this issue.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed solution to the identified limitation.

claim: Animals were rewarded to report only the visual stimulus and were incentivized to ignore the optostim signal.
source: A key feature of our experiment was that the animals were rewarded to report only the visual stimulus, and were thus incentivized to ignore the optostim signal.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: In most previous optostim behavioral experiments in NHPs, animals were rewarded for reporting the optostim signal itself.
source: In contrast, in most previous optostim behavioral experiments, NHPs were rewarded for reporting the optostim signal itself (e.g., Ju et al., 2018; May et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the current study, with citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies that rewarded animals for reporting optostim do not directly test for perceptual substitution by optostimulation.
source: Such studies do not directly test for perceptual substitution by optostimulation.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous experimental approaches.

claim: Monkeys show large perceptual masking effects of optostim when the visual target is presented at the receptive field of optogenetically stimulated neurons.
source: Our finding that monkeys show large perceptual masking effects of optostim when the visual target is presented at the receptive field of the optogenetically stimulated neurons, indicates that the optostim-evoked response is largely inseparable perceptually from the visual-evoked response
evidence: This is stated as a finding and interpretation from the experiments.

claim: Optostim can substitute for a visual mask even when the animal is motivated to ignore it.
source: and that optostim can substitute for a visual mask even when the animal is motivated to ignore it.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of V1 is altering the monkeys' perception of the visual target in a way consistent with visual masking.
source: Thus, our results reveal that optogenetic stimulation of V1 is altering the monkeys' perception of the visual target in a way that is consistent with visual masking.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: The masking effect of optostim is spatially selective, similar to visual masking.
source: Similar to visual masking, this effect is spatially selective
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Monkeys do not seem to be able to learn to compensate for the presence of optogenetic stimulation.
source: and the monkeys do not seem to be able to learn to compensate for the presence of the optogenetic (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: The target size (0.33° FWHM) was smaller than the average receptive field of V1 neurons at these eccentricities (0.58° FWHM).
source: Because the target size (0.33° FWHM) was smaller than the average receptive field of V1 neurons at these eccentricities (0.58° FWHM; Chen et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the experimental design, with citation to previous work.

claim: The cortical area responding to the target was approximately equal to the cortical point image and had an area at half max of ~4 mm2.
source: the cortical area responding to the target was approximately equal to the cortical point image, and had an area at half max of ~4 mm2 (Palmer et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on the target size, with citation to previous work.

claim: The cortical area responding to the target is about twice the size of the area at half max of the optostimulation-evoked responses.
source: which is about twice the size of the area at half max of the optostimulation-evoked responses (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison based on measurements, supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: Optostim likely evoked a response in a cortical area smaller than the response evoked by the visual target.
source: Therefore, it is likely that optostim evoked a response in a cortical area that is smaller than the response evoked by the visual target
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the size comparisons.

claim: Even within the overlapping region, optostim and visual target likely elicited responses with different spatial profiles.
source: and that even within the overlapping region the two stimuli elicited responses with different spatial profiles.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the different spatial extents of the responses.

claim: In visual masking, the mask does not have to be identical to the target to lead to a perceptual masking effect.
source: In this respect, optostim masking is similar to visual masking, where the mask does not have to be identical to the target to lead to a perceptual masking effect.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to known properties of visual masking.

claim: Virally delivered genes can lead to stable foreign protein expression for extended periods in humans and NHPs.
source: First, while previous results suggest that virally delivered genes can lead to stable foreign protein expression for extended periods in humans and NHPs
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge from previous results.

claim: Stable co-expression of reporters and actuators was documented for periods exceeding the lifespan of the chambers (typically >2 years).
source: we document here stable co-expression of reporters and actuators for periods that exceed the lifespan of our chambers (typically >2 years; Monkey T's chamber is still active more than 30 months from chamber opening with continued stable expression of GCaMP and C1V1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: Effective optostim at low-power densities is important for stable, long-term use in future implantable oBCIs.
source: Second, effective optostim at low-power densities is important for stable, long-term use in future implantable oBCIs.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the importance of the findings.

claim: Behavioral and physiological effects of optogenetics in macaques typically require high stimulation light power densities.
source: Behavioral and physiological effects of optogenetics in macaques typically require high stimulation light power densities (e.g., Ruiz et al., 2013; Nassi et al., 2015; Jazayeri et al., 2012; though see Ju et al., 2018 for a demonstration of a behavioral effect at low power)
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge from previous studies, with citations.

claim: High power optostim raises concerns about possible tissue damage.
source: leading to concerns about possible tissue damage (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016)
evidence: This is stated as a concern from previous work, with citation.

claim: High light level may limit the use of future implantable devices due to power requirements.
source: High light level may also limit the use of future implantable devices due to power requirements.
evidence: This is stated as a practical concern for future applications.

claim: Very low optical power levels are sufficient to elicit reliable neural responses within the biologically relevant dynamic range.
source: We demonstrate that very low optical power levels are sufficient to elicit reliable neural responses within the biologically relevant dynamic range of neural responses to visual stimuli and to replace a visual mask with optostim in a visual detection task.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: The optostim power densities reported overestimate the actual effective power densities used in the study.
source: In fact, the optostim power densities reported here overestimate the actual effective power densities used in our study.
evidence: This is stated as a clarification about the reported power densities.

claim: The optostim light was flashed with a duty cycle of 22%, so the time average power density was only a fraction of the maximum.
source: The optostim light was flashed with a duty cycle of 22%; therefore, the time average of the power density was only a fraction of the maximum power density reported.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the stimulation parameters.

claim: Preliminary results suggest that optostim-evoked neural responses are proportional to the time average of the power density.
source: Preliminary results suggest that the optostim-evoked neural responses are proportional to the time average of the power density of the stimulation light and are relatively insensitive to the temporal parameters of the stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a preliminary finding supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: Orange light at 580 nm was used to stimulate C1V1 to prevent contamination of calcium imaging.
source: In addition, we used orange light at 580 nm to stimulate C1V1 in order to prevent the optostim light from contaminating our simultaneous calcium imaging.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental design choice.

claim: The orange light at 580 nm is shifted from the peak excitation of C1V1 (~530 nm), which further reduced the effective power of optostim.
source: This orange light is shifted from the peak excitation of C1V1 (~530 nm) and this further reduced the effective power of the optostim.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why the effective power was lower than reported.

claim: Clear sublinear interaction between GCaMP-measured neural responses elicited by visual stimuli and by direct optogenetic stimulation in V1 was observed.
source: Our results reveal clear sublinear interaction between GCaMP-measured neural responses elicited by visual stimuli and by direct optogenetic stimulation in V1.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: The observed sublinear interaction is likely to reflect a sublinear interaction at the level of V1 spiking activity.
source: Therefore, the observed sublinear interaction is likely to reflect a sublinear interaction at the level of V1 spiking activity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the known relationship between GCaMP signals and spiking.

claim: Pilot electrophysiological results demonstrate strong sublinear interaction between visual- and optogenetic-evoked multi-unit spiking activity at the C1V1 site in Monkey L.
source: Consistent with this possibility, pilot electrophysiological results demonstrate strong sublinear interaction between visual- and optogenetic-evoked multi-unit spiking activity at the C1V1 site in Monkey L (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a preliminary finding from pilot experiments.

claim: Neural responses to visual stimuli are highly nonlinear and consistent with luminance and contrast gain control.
source: While it is well known that neural responses to visual stimuli are highly nonlinear and are consistent with luminance and contrast gain control (e.g., Albrecht and Hamilton, 1982; Purpura et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to previous work.

claim: Some of the nonlinearities observed in V1 response are likely inherited from its ascending inputs.
source: some of the nonlinearities observed in V1 response are likely to be inherited from its ascending inputs.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on knowledge of visual system organization.

claim: It is unclear how much of the gain control is implemented in V1.
source: It is therefore unclear how much of the gain control is implemented in V1
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field.

claim: The results are consistent with a significant contribution of V1 circuits to gain control or normalization.
source: Our results are consistent with a significant contribution of V1 circuits to gain control, or normalization.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Some of the observed sublinearity could be due to V1 neurons being driven to their physiological limit by optostim.
source: However, we cannot rule out that some of the observed sublinearity could be due to V1 neurons that are driven to their physiological limit by optostim.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative explanation that cannot be ruled out.

claim: The observed sublinear interaction is consistent with findings from a study by Nassi et al. using electrophysiology in fixating macaque V1.
source: The observed sublinear interaction between visual- and optogenetic-evoked GCaMP responses in V1 is consistent with recent findings from a study by Nassi et al., where they used electrophysiology to study the interactions between visual- and optogenetics-evoked responses in fixating macaque V1 (Nassi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work, with citation.

claim: In the Nassi et al. study, light power densities required to elicit optogenetic-evoked responses were one to two orders of magnitude higher than in the current study.
source: However, in that study, the light power densities required to elicit optogenetic-evoked responses were one to two orders of magnitude higher than in the current study.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work.

claim: High power densities raise concerns regarding tissue heating, which could affect the nature of interactions between visual- and optogenetic-evoked responses.
source: Such high power densities raise concerns regarding tissue heating, which could affect the nature of the interactions between visual- and optogenetic-evoked responses in V1.
evidence: This is stated as a concern about previous work using high power densities.

claim: The current results significantly extend the results of Nassi et al. and provide an important confirmation of their main finding.
source: Therefore, our results, in addition to demonstrating a novel perceptual interaction between visual and optogenetic stimulation in V1, significantly extend the results of Nassi et al., and provide an important confirmation of their main finding.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the contribution relative to previous work.

claim: Multiple factors could contribute to different sensitivity to optostim observed in different studies, including differences in opsin expression levels.
source: Multiple factors could contribute to the different sensitivity to optostim observed in the two studies, including differences in opsin expression levels, differences in the size of the neural population stimulated and/or monitored in the two studies, and difference in the visual stimulus (drifting gratings vs. a small Gaussian target in the current study).
evidence: This is stated as possible explanations for differences between studies.

claim: A recent study by Andrei et al. used optostim and electrophysiology to examine perceptual and neural effects of V1 optostim in monkeys detecting very dim visual gratings.
source: Our results contrast with those of a recent study which used optostim and electrophysiology to examine the perceptual and neural effect of V1 optostim in monkeys performing detection of very dim visual gratings on a dark background (more than two orders of magnitude darker than in the current study; Andrei et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work, with citation.

claim: In the Andrei et al. study, optostim caused a small improvement in detection when stimulus orientation was near the preferred orientation of optostimulated neurons.
source: In that study, optostim caused a small improvement in detection when stimulus orientation was near the preferred orientation of the optostimulated neurons, but had no effect when it was far.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings from previous work.

claim: In the Andrei et al. study, electrophysiological measurements revealed no interaction between average visual- and optogenetic-evoked responses.
source: Electrophysiological measurements revealed no interaction between average visual- and optogenetic-evoked responses
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings from previous work.

claim: In the Andrei et al. study, optostimulation induced a reduction in noise correlations only when stimulus orientation was near the preferred orientation.
source: but instead, optostimulation induced a reduction in noise correlations between pairs of neurons only when stimulus orientation was near the preferred orientation of the optostimulated neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings from previous work.

claim: The contrasting results between the current study and Andrei et al. are not surprising given the different regimes of cortical activity examined.
source: These contrasting results are not surprising given that the two studies examined the interactions between visual and optogenetic stimulation under very different regimes of cortical activity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the differences between studies.

claim: Low-power optostim can elicit GCaMP population responses that far exceed the responses to Gaussian targets.
source: We find that even though optostim engages gain control mechanisms in V1, low-power optostim can elicit GCaMP population responses that far exceed the responses to our Gaussian targets (Figure 5G and H; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: Optostim driving V1 population responses beyond any visual stimulus does not necessarily follow from the observation that it exceeds responses to Gaussian targets.
source: This is an interesting observation, but it does not necessarily imply that optostim can drive V1 population responses to a range that exceeds the population response to any visual stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as a clarification about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Population responses to Gaussian targets can increase significantly by increasing target amplitude while lowering background luminance.
source: First, even for the small Gaussian stimuli used in the current study, it is likely that population responses can increase significantly by increasing the target amplitude while lowering the background luminance.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on knowledge of visual responses.

claim: The background luminance in the current study was high relative to the target amplitude, so the response evoked by Gaussian targets was moderate.
source: Because the background luminance in the current study was high relative to the target amplitude, the response evoked by our Gaussian targets was moderate.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the moderate responses observed.

claim: Other classes of visual stimuli may elicit population responses higher than the response to a Gaussian target.
source: Second, it is possible that other classes of visual stimuli can elicit population responses that are higher than the response to a Gaussian target.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility.

claim: Localized low spatial frequency stimuli are surprisingly effective at driving V1 population activity.
source: However, we recently found that localized low spatial frequency stimuli are surprisingly effective at driving V1 population activity (Benvenuti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent work by the authors, with citation.

claim: Widefield calcium imaging signals reflect the weighted sum of neural activity pooled over a Gaussian-shaped region with a space constant of ~0.2 mm.
source: Widefield calcium imaging signals at each cortical location reflect the weighted sum of neural activity pooled over a Gaussian-shaped region with a space constant of ~0.2 mm (Seidemann et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous work by the authors, with citations.

claim: GCaMP-evoked neural response reflects the pooled spiking activity of a large population of neurons with diverse tuning properties.
source: Therefore, the GCaMP-evoked neural response reflects the pooled spiking activity of a large population of neurons with diverse tuning properties.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the spatial pooling properties of widefield imaging.

claim: Gaussian stimuli are suboptimal for individual V1 neurons because they are unoriented.
source: The Gaussian stimuli used here are suboptimal for individual V1 neurons because they are unoriented.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the stimulus properties relative to V1 neuron tuning.

claim: Gaussian stimuli can lead to robust population response in V1 because they activate a large fraction of neurons at the corresponding retinotopic location.
source: Even though they drive individual neurons weakly, they can lead to robust population response in V1 because they activate a large fraction of the neurons at the corresponding retinotopic location.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why Gaussian stimuli are effective at the population level.

claim: Visual stimuli optimized for a subset of V1 neurons activate strongly a small subpopulation but activate poorly most other neurons.
source: In contrast, visual stimuli that are optimized for a subset of V1 neurons, such as oriented Gabor patches, activate strongly a small subpopulation but activate poorly most other neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to explain the effectiveness of Gaussian stimuli at the population level.

claim: Gaussian targets could be surprisingly effective at driving locally pooled V1 population responses.
source: Therefore, Gaussian targets could be surprisingly effective at driving locally pooled V1 population responses.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the reasoning about population responses.

claim: Detection thresholds for Gaussians are comparable to detection thresholds for Gabor patches.
source: Consistent with this possibility, detection thresholds for Gaussians are comparable to detection thresholds for Gabor patches (Watson and Ahumada, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence from previous work, with citation.

claim: A larger masking effect of optostim on V1 neural detection sensitivity than on behavioral sensitivity was observed.
source: Our results reveal a larger masking effect of optostim on V1 neural sensitivity than on behavioral sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: In both monkeys, low-power optostim can effectively erase the visual-evoked responses from GCaMP measurements (reduce by 100%).
source: In both monkeys, low-power optostim can effectively erase the visual-evoked responses from our GCaMP measurements (i.e., reduce target-evoked responses by 100%; Figure 6B and D)
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by data in Figures 6B and D.

claim: Both monkeys could still perform the detection task with optostim, albeit with elevated thresholds.
source: yet both monkeys could still perform the detection task with optostim (albeit with elevated thresholds).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Widefield GCaMP imaging is not capturing all of the visual signals available for detection in V1.
source: These results suggest that our widefield GCaMP imaging is not capturing all of the visual signals that are available for detection in V1.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the discrepancy between neural and behavioral effects.

claim: The incomplete capture of visual signals could reflect visual responses that spread laterally over a larger region than the area affected by optostim.
source: This could reflect visual responses that spread laterally over a larger region than the area affected by optostim
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the incomplete capture of visual signals.

claim: The incomplete capture could reflect target-evoked signals deeper in the cortex that are inaccessible to widefield imaging.
source: and/or target-evoked signals that are deeper in the cortex and are therefore inaccessible to widefield imaging.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the incomplete capture of visual signals.

claim: Some target-related signals present at the single neuron level may be eliminated by indiscriminate pooling of widefield imaging.
source: In addition, it is possible that even within the affected region, some target-related signals that are present at the single neuron level are eliminated by the indiscriminate pooling of widefield imaging over large populations of neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the incomplete capture of visual signals.

claim: Additional research is needed to achieve a more complete understanding of the nonlinearities between visual and optostim responses and their underlying mechanisms.
source: While our study and previous findings (Nassi et al., 2015) reveal clear nonlinear interaction between visual- and optostim-evoked responses in V1, additional research is needed in order to achieve a more complete understanding of these nonlinearities and their underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as a direction for future research.

claim: The study demonstrates the importance of combining optogenetic stimulation and optical imaging to calibrate stimulation in a biologically-relevant regime.
source: Our study demonstrates the importance of combining optogenetic stimulation and optical imaging to calibrate the stimulation so that the evoked neural response falls in a biological-relevant regime.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the methodological approach.

claim: Future studies could use real-time close-loop feedback to optimize the stimulation pattern.
source: Future studies could take further advantage of this simultaneous read-write capability and use real-time close-loop feedback to optimize the stimulation pattern.
evidence: This is stated as a direction for future research.

claim: Spatially homogeneous optogenetic light stimulation was used to generate a localized mask of optostim-evoked neural responses.
source: In the current study, we used spatially homogeneous optogenetic light stimulation to generate a localized mask of optostim-evoked neural responses.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the current approach.

claim: An important future direction is to use a projector to generate arbitrary spatiotemporal patterns of light stimulation.
source: An important future direction is to replace the current source of the optogenetic light stimulation with a projector that would allow one to generate arbitrary spatiotemporal patterns of light stimulation (Huang et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated as a direction for future research, with citations to relevant technology.

claim: Patterned optostim could be used to mimic the pattern of population responses elicited by visual stimuli at relevant topographic scales.
source: thus furthering the ability to mimic with optostim the pattern of population responses elicited by visual stimuli at relevant topographic scales such as retinotopy and orientation columns.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of patterned optostim.

claim: Patterned optostim could be used to causally test specific hypotheses regarding the role of topography in sensory cortical representations.
source: This form of patterned optostim could be used in the future to causally test specific hypotheses regarding the role of topography in sensory cortical representations.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of patterned optostim.

claim: Two macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta, male, 7–8 years of age, weighing 11 and 7 kg) were used in the experiments.
source: Two macaque monkeys (Monkey L and Monkey T; Macaca mulatta, male, 7–8 years of age during experimentation, weighing 11 and 7 kg, respectively)
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Monkeys were implanted with a custom recording chamber placed over cranial windows for direct physical and optical access to V1.
source: were implanted with a custom recording chamber placed over cranial windows for direct physical and optical access to the awake macaque primary visual cortex (V1; Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the surgical preparation.

claim: Each monkey was injected with ~2 µl of GCaMP6f viral vector per injection site.
source: For neural reading, each monkey was first injected with ~2 µl of a GCaMP6f (Chen et al., 2013) viral vector per injection site
evidence: This is stated as a description of the viral injection procedure.

claim: A transparent artificial dura made of silicone was used to protect the brain while allowing optical access for imaging.
source: A transparent artificial dura made of silicone was used to protect the brain while allowing optical access for imaging (Arieli et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the surgical preparation, with citation.

claim: The combination of 50 mm and 85 mm objective lenses provided 1.7× magnification, imaging approximately an 8 × 8 mm2 area of cortex.
source: The combination of a 50 mm fixed-focus objective lens (cortex end, Nikkor 50 mm f/1.2) and an 85 mm fixed-focus objective lens (Canon EF 85 mm f/1.2 L USM) provided 1.7× magnification, corresponding to imaging approximately an 8 × 8 mm2 area of the cortex (using PCO Edge 4.2 CLHS sCMOS camera).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the imaging system specifications.

claim: Imaging was conducted with minimal GCaMP illumination power at a low camera saturation level (1–5%) and a low 20 Hz frame rate.
source: Therefore, imaging was conducted with minimal GCaMP illumination power (0.05 mW/mm2 in Monkey L and 0.01 mW/mm2 in Monkey T) at a low camera saturation level (1–5%) and a low 20 Hz frame rate.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the imaging parameters.

claim: Data acquisition was time locked to the animal's heartbeat (EKG QR up-stroke).
source: Data acquisition was time locked to the animal's heartbeat (EKG QR up-stroke).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data acquisition procedure.

claim: Raw images were captured at 2048 × 2048 resolution and binned to 512 × 512.
source: Raw images were captured at 2048 × 2048 resolution, binned to 512 × 512.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the image acquisition parameters.

claim: The Gaussian target was positioned at 1.5° eccentricity (–35° from the right-hand horizontal meridian) in Monkey L at the C1V1 site.
source: The target was positioned at corresponding retinotopic coordinates of the C1V1 expression site, which was 1.5° eccentricity (–35° from the right-hand horizontal meridian) in Monkey L
evidence: This is stated as a description of the stimulus location.

claim: The Gaussian target was positioned at 2.7° eccentricity (–46° from the right-hand horizontal meridian) in Monkey T at the C1V1 site.
source: and was 2.7° eccentricity (–46° from the right-hand horizontal meridian) in Monkey T.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the stimulus location.

claim: For the GCaMP-only experiments, the visual stimulus was centered at 2.0° eccentricity (–45° from the horizontal meridian) for Monkey L.
source: For the GCaMP-only experiments, the visuals stimulus was centered at the retinotopic location corresponding to a nearby cortical site with only GCaMP6f expression (no C1V1 injection/expression). This was 2.0° eccentricity (–45° from the horizontal meridian) for Monkey L
evidence: This is stated as a description of the stimulus location for control experiments.

claim: For the GCaMP-only experiments, the visual stimulus was centered at 2.0° eccentricity (–40° from the horizontal meridian) for Monkey T.
source: and 2.0° eccentricity (–40° from the horizontal meridian) for Monkey T.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the stimulus location for control experiments.

claim: The distances between the centers of the C1V1 and GCaMP-only sites were 3 mm in Monkey L (0.6° distance between receptive field centers).
source: The distances between the centers of the C1V1 and GCaMP-only sites were 3 mm in Monkey L (corresponding to 0.6° distance between receptive field centers)
evidence: This is stated as a description of the spatial arrangement of injection sites.

claim: The distances between the centers of the C1V1 and GCaMP-only sites were 4 mm in Monkey T (0.7° distance between receptive field centers).
source: and 4 mm in Monkey T (corresponding to 0.7° distance between receptive field centers).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the spatial arrangement of injection sites.

claim: The visual target at the C1V1 and GCaMP-only sites in each monkey did not overlap in the visual field.
source: While the Gaussian targets at the C1V1 and the GCaMP-only sites in each monkey did not overlap in the visual field
evidence: This is stated as a description of the spatial arrangement of stimuli.

claim: The population receptive fields at the C1V1 and GCaMP-only locations partially overlapped.
source: the population receptive fields at these two locations partially overlapped, so that the visual target at one location partially activated some of the neurons at the other location.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the receptive field overlap.

claim: Each trial began with fixation on a bright 0.1° square.
source: Each trial began with fixation on a bright 0.1° square.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral task.

claim: An auditory tone and dimming of the fixation square cued the monkey to the start of the detection task trial.
source: An auditory tone and the dimming of the fixation square cued the monkey to the start of the detection task trial
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral task.

claim: 250 ms after the cue, the Gaussian target was presented on 50% of the trials.
source: 250 ms later, the Gaussian target was presented on 50% of the trials.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral task timing.

claim: Monkeys were trained to stay at fixation on target-absent trials or make a saccade to the target position on target-present trials.
source: The monkeys were trained to stay at the fixation cue on target-absent trials or make a saccade to, and hold gaze (for 150 ms) at, the target position to indicate target detection (with a 75 ms minimum allowed reaction time).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral task requirements.

claim: When the target was present, it remained on screen for a maximum of 250 ms or was extinguished upon the monkey's saccade.
source: When the target was present, it remained on screen for a maximum of 250 ms or was extinguished upon the monkeys' saccade (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral task timing.

claim: The monkey was given 600 ms to make the saccade or to hold fixation.
source: The monkey was given 600 ms to make the saccade or to hold fixation
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral task timing.

claim: The monkey was rewarded on correct choices (correct reject on target-absent trials and hit on target-present trials).
source: and was subsequently rewarded on correct choices (stay [correct reject] on target-absent trials, and saccade to target [hit] on target-present trials).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the reward contingency.

claim: The size of the fixation window was 1.8–2.4° × 1.8–2.8°.
source: The size of the fixation window (X × Y) was 1.8–2.4° × 1.8–2.8°
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral task parameters.

claim: The saccade target window was 2.4–3.0° × 2.4–4.5°.
source: and the saccade target window was 2.4–3.0° × 2.4–4.5°.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral task parameters.

claim: The visual target was presented 250 ms after the temporal cue, whereas optostim was applied 290 ms after the cue.
source: The visual target was presented 250 ms after the temporal cue, whereas the optostim was applied 290 ms after the cue.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the timing of visual and optogenetic stimulation.

claim: The 40 ms delay in optostim ensured that optostim-evoked V1 response coincides approximately with the onset of the visual-target-evoked response.
source: This 40 ms delay in optostim insured that optostim-evoked V1 response coincides approximately with the onset of the visual-target-evoked response on target-present trials (Figure 5E and G).
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for the timing delay, supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: Optostim was presented in pulses of 5 ms spaced every 22.5 ms (~44 Hz).
source: Optostim was presented in pulses of 5 ms spaced every 22.5 ms (~44 Hz)
evidence: This is stated as a description of the optostim parameters.

claim: Optostim was extinguished after 210 ms (coinciding with maximum visual target duration) or on the onset of saccade.
source: and was extinguished after 210 ms (coinciding with maximum visual target duration) or on the onset of saccade (coinciding with extinguishing the visual target).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the optostim timing.

claim: The V1 response is approximately proportional to the time average of the optostim power density based on pilot studies.
source: Pilot studies, in which we compared widefield GCaMP response to pulsed and continuous optostim, suggest that the V1 response is approximately proportional to the time average of the optostim power density (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from pilot studies, supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: The effective power density was about 25% of the peak power density reported.
source: These pilot studies suggest that the effective power density was about 25% of the peak power density reported here.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the pilot studies.

claim: Power density was measured through all optical filters/apparatus at the plane of the imaged cortex.
source: Power density (in mW/mm2) was measured through all the optical filters/apparatus at the plane of the imaged cortex, with the total power read from a light meter (ThorLabs PM100D with S170C sensor) and divided by the illuminated area
evidence: This is stated as a description of the power density measurement method.

claim: The illuminated area was a circular disk with diameter 13 mm for C1V1 optostim light and 19 mm for GCaMP light.
source: (circular disk: diameter 13 mm for C1V1 optostim light, and 19 mm for GCaMP light).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the illumination parameters.

claim: The visual stimulus was presented on a Sony CRT (1024 × 768 @ 100 Hz) distanced 108 cm from the animal.
source: The visual stimulus was presented on a Sony CRT (1024 × 768 @ 100 Hz), distanced 108 cm from the animal (50 pixels-per-degree), with mean luminance 50 cd/m2.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the visual display parameters.

claim: For each trial, an image sequence was captured for a total of 1.2 s including pre-stimulus and post-stimulus frames.
source: For each trial, an image sequence was captured for a total of 1.2 s including pre-stimulus and post-stimulus frames.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the imaging data collection.

claim: Image stabilization is a new routine used to de-accentuate blood vessel edges in the ΔF/F response map caused by micro movements.
source: Image stabilization is a new routine we use to de-accentuate blood vessel edges in the ΔF/F response map caused by micro movements of the camera and/or the cortex during imaging.
evidence: This is stated as a description of a new analysis method.

claim: The average response over three frames from 50 to 200 ms post-stimulus was used to represent the neural signal pertaining to the animal's behavioral decision.
source: The average response over the three frames from 50 to 200 ms post-stimulus was used to represent the neural signal pertaining to the animal's behavioral decision.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the analysis approach.

claim: Responses beyond 50-200 ms were not used as they are generally post-saccade.
source: Responses beyond this range were not used as they are generally post-saccade (median saccade times were 149 and 204 ms, respectively, for Monkey L and T; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the analysis window, supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: The Naka-Rushton function was used to characterize neural response as a function of visual stimulus contrast.
source: The Naka-Rushton function was used to characterize neural response as a function of visual stimulus contrast (c)
evidence: This is stated as a description of the analysis method.

claim: Two animals were examined to verify the consistency of experimental approach and results.
source: Two animals were examined to verify the consistency of experimental approach and results.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental design.

claim: Multiple recordings were made from the same animals.
source: Multiple recordings were made from the same animals.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental design.

claim: No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size.
source: The number of recordings was based on previous experience; no statistical method was used to predetermine sample size.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental design approach.

claim: Each experiment condition was repeated at least three times in separate days in each animal.
source: Each experiment condition (optostim power level × cortical site) was repeated at least three times (in separate days) in each animal, pairing with a visual-only block each day.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental design.

claim: The number of trials collected each day varied between 200 and 600 trials (typically 400) depending on the animal's motivation.
source: The number of trials collected each day varied between 200 and 600 trials (typically 400) depending on the animal's motivation.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data collection.

claim: Trials were excluded when the monkey did not follow the task routine, when EKG signal was noisy, and when excessive motion artifact was detected.
source: Trials were excluded when the monkey did not follow the task routine, when EKG signal was noisy, and when excessive motion artifact was detected in the imaged data.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Where bootstrapped resampling was applied, the data was resampled 1000 times with replacement within trials of the same stimulus condition.
source: Where bootstrapped resampling was applied, the data was resampled 1000 times with replacement within trials of the same stimulus condition (visual target amplitude and optostim level).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the statistical analysis method.
